problem: Prior VQA answers questions passively from a fixed image or video. Prior embodied or language-grounded agents trained with a single monolithic RL controller (A3C-style, as in Chaplot et al. / Hill et al. / Zhu et al.) cannot handle the large, diverse state and action space needed to navigate, open containers, remember what was seen and then answer. They also generalize poorly to unseen scenes.
motivation: Household-robot questions such as 'Do we need more milk?' or 'How many boxes of cookies?' require the agent to navigate, interact (e.g. open the fridge or cabinets), and keep long-term spatial-semantic memory of what is where. The authors observe that these subtasks are fairly independent and work at different time scales. That suggests a hierarchical factorization with an explicit semantic map, where each controller can be pretrained separately using oracle versions of the others.
key_idea: Factorize interactive QA into a high-level RL Planner that calls low-level controllers (Navigator, Scanner, Detector, Manipulator, Answerer). The controllers share an explicit semantic spatial map that an Egocentric Spatial GRU writes only in a local egocentric window.
insight: Persistent spatial-semantic memory plus hierarchical control is what makes the task learnable. The monolithic A3C baseline scores at or below chance even with GT detections (48.59 / 24.53 / 49.84 vs MLA 50 / 25 / 50), because detections do not persist and it never learns when to answer. The ablations (Table 3) show two components are each necessary. Removing the question from the Planner drops HIMN-GT to chance (50.00 / 24.50 / 50.25), so the Planner uses the question to decide where to explore and what to open. Removing the supervised loss on invalid/viable actions also gives chance-level accuracy (49.84 / 24.84 / 50.00) and raises invalid actions from about 6% to about 53-56%. Perception is the main bottleneck: GT detections and depth raise Existence from 68.47 to 86.56, and an oracle navigator mostly helps Counting (35.31 to 48.44). The seen vs unseen gap is small (e.g. 73.68 vs 68.47 on Existence), so the semantic map generalizes across rooms.
method: Egocentric Spatial GRU (esGRU): the global memory is a 3D tensor over a 2D floor grid. Each cell holds object-detection probabilities, free-space (occupancy) probability, coverage and navigation intent. Each step, a local egocentric window is swapped into the GRU hidden state, updated from current inputs, and swapped back at the agent's location, which avoids corrupting distant memory. Low-level controllers can read and write; the Planner is read-only.

Planner (A3C): a GRU takes the CNN-encoded current view and the previous action. Its output is combined with the question embedding and an embedding of the nearby spatial memory to output a policy over 32 discrete high-level actions and a value. The actions are: Navigator to a cell of a 5x5 grid in front of the agent, Scanner direction, Manipulator open/close, and Answer. Rewards: fixed reward or penalty for a correct or incorrect answer, a per-step time penalty, an invalid-action penalty, and an intermediate coverage reward.

Action-validity auxiliary loss: the Planner also predicts which high-level actions are viable in the current state, supervised on all actions. This propagates gradients through the whole action space rather than only the chosen action, speeding convergence and cutting invalid actions.

Navigator: esGRU predicts a local 5x5 occupancy grid from the current view (supervised with sigmoid cross-entropy) to update the global occupancy map. A* replans the shortest path after each update, the Navigator calls the Scanner for wide views, and it predicts a termination signal for unreachable goals.

Scanner / Detector / Manipulator: the Scanner rotates the camera up, down, left or right and calls the Detector on each new image. The Detector is YOLOv3 fine-tuned on AI2-THOR training scenes; FRCN monocular depth (Laina et al.) projects detections to the ground plane, and they enter memory by moving average. The Manipulator opens or closes the object nearest the image center. Scanner and Manipulator have no learned parameters.

Answerer: the question vector is tiled to the map size and concatenated depthwise with the full spatial memory, then passed through 4 conv + max-pool layers, a spatial sum, 2 FC layers and a softmax over answer choices. Invoking it ends the episode.

Training: each controller is pretrained separately with oracles for the others. The Planner uses a GT shortest-path navigator and GT object info, the Navigator uses random start/goal pairs, the Answerer uses GT partial semantic maps, and the Detector is fine-tuned YOLOv3. The whole system is then fine-tuned jointly end-to-end.

setting.backbone: HIMN: GRU-based Planner trained with A3C, esGRU spatial memory, conv Answerer (trained from scratch), YOLOv3 detector (fine-tuned on AI2-THOR), FRCN depth estimator (Laina et al.), A* planner
setting.training_data: IQUAD V1 train split: 25 AI2-THOR kitchen rooms and 76,800 scene configurations, i.e. 25,600 questions each for Existence, Counting and Spatial Relationships (templated, auto-generated, balanced). YOLOv3 is fine-tuned on AI2-THOR training scenes.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB (depth estimated by FRCN; GT depth only in oracle variants) + templated question
setting.action_space: hierarchical: 32 discrete high-level Planner actions (navigate to a cell in a 5x5 grid ahead / scan direction / open-close / answer). Low-level grid actions: move ahead 25 cm, rotate 90° left/right, look up/down 30°, open/close.
setting.privileged: Main model: none explicitly stated beyond grid-world movement; the agent's grid location appears to be assumed known for writing into the egocentric memory. Ablation variants use GT object detections + GT depth, and an oracle shortest-path navigator (HIMN-GT).

numbers_note: The benchmark is the paper's own IQUAD V1 (not in the canonical list). The metric is Top-1 QA accuracy per question type plus average episode length in steps; there is no SR or SPL. The 'val-seen' label is an approximation for the paper's 'Seen' evaluation on training rooms with new configurations. Other ablation rows in Table 3 are not listed here: 'Question not given to planner' 50.00/24.50/50.25 and 'No loss on invalid actions' 49.84/24.84/50.00 (Existence/Counting/SpatialRel accuracy). The main A3C baseline is given GT detections, while main HIMN uses YOLO. The human baseline is a small sample.
results: On unseen IQUAD V1 test rooms, HIMN with YOLO detections reaches 68.47 (Existence), 30.43 (Counting) and 58.67 (Spatial Relationships) accuracy. It clearly beats the A3C single-controller baseline even though that baseline is given GT detections (48.59 / 24.53 / 49.84, at or below the MLA chance baseline of 50 / 25 / 50). With GT perception and an oracle navigator (HIMN-GT), accuracy rises to 88.60 / 48.44 / 72.50, still far below humans (90 / 80 / 90). Humans also need far shorter episodes (roughly 43-82 vs roughly 318-926 steps). Seen-room accuracy is only a few points higher than unseen.
limitations: The 2D semantic map cannot tell an object inside a container from one on top of it, which limits spatial-relationship questions.

Exploration is inefficient: episodes of hundreds of steps vs about 43-82 for humans. Accuracy on Counting stays low, and performance depends heavily on detector and navigator quality (large gains with GT oracles).

Templated questions with a 70-word vocabulary, kitchen-only rooms (25 train / 5 test) and a grid-world simulator with discrete actions. There are no real-robot experiments and the language model would not handle arbitrary questions.
